questions.question: In a singly linked list, what does each node hold besides its own data?
options: References to both the next and the previous node
Its own index within the list
A reference to the next node only
A reference to the list's head node
questions.explanation: A singly linked node stores its value plus one next reference. Previous links exist only in doubly linked lists, and nodes never know their own index.

questions.question: Which interfaces does java.util.LinkedList implement?
questions.explanation: LinkedList implements List and Deque (hence Queue too). It deliberately does not implement RandomAccess, because indexed access is O(n).

questions.question: What is the worst-case cost of get(int index) on a java.util.LinkedList of size n?
questions.explanation: There is no backing index array, so LinkedList walks node by node starting from the nearer end: about n/2 steps, which is O(n).

questions.question: On a java.util.LinkedList, push(e) does exactly the same thing as which call?
questions.explanation: Deque.push is specified as addFirst, so push/pop on a LinkedList give stack behaviour that grows and shrinks at the head.

questions.question: Which method removes and returns the head of a LinkedList, returning null when the list is empty?
questions.explanation: poll() removes and returns the head and yields null when empty, while remove(), element() and pop() throw NoSuchElementException.

questions.question: On an empty LinkedList, how does getFirst() differ from peekFirst()?
options: getFirst() throws NoSuchElementException, peekFirst() gives null
questions.explanation: The get/remove/element family throws NoSuchElementException on an empty list, while the peek/poll family signals emptiness by returning null.

questions.question: Can java.util.LinkedList store null elements?
options: Only when added through add(), not addFirst()
Yes, but only one null per list
questions.explanation: LinkedList permits null and duplicate elements, unlike ArrayDeque. That is why a null returned by poll() can be ambiguous.

questions.question: How is java.util.LinkedList implemented internally?
options: As a growable array with a linked view
As a circular singly linked list
questions.explanation: Each internal node holds item, next and prev, and the list keeps first and last pointers, so operations at either end are O(1).

questions.question: Which field declaration gives this generic node a type-safe link to the following node?
questions.explanation: The link must point to another node carrying the same element type, so the field type is Node<T>. T next would store a value, not a node.

questions.question: What is the correct way to delete matching elements while iterating a LinkedList?
options: Call list.remove(e) inside an enhanced for loop
Call it.remove() before each call to it.next()
Call it.next(), then it.remove() on the same Iterator
Set matching entries to null and filter them later
questions.explanation: Iterator.remove() deletes the element last returned by next() and keeps expectedModCount in sync, so iteration continues safely.

questions.question: What are the time complexities of contains(o) and indexOf(o) on java.util.LinkedList?
questions.explanation: Both walk the chain from the head comparing elements until a match is found, so both are O(n) in the worst case.

questions.question: In a doubly linked list with sentinels, you already hold a reference to an interior node. What does this unlink cost?
options: O(1); only a fixed number of references change
O(n); the previous node has to be searched for
O(n); every following index must be renumbered
questions.explanation: A doubly linked node knows both neighbours, so unlinking is a constant number of pointer writes regardless of list size.

questions.question: The list starts as [a, b, c]. What does this ListIterator loop print?
questions.explanation: ListIterator.add inserts just before the implicit cursor, that is right after the element next() returned, and the new element is not visited again.

questions.question: A custom singly linked list keeps only a head pointer. What does appending to the end cost?
options: O(n), because the last node must be walked to
questions.explanation: Without a tail pointer the whole chain must be traversed to find the last node, so append is O(n); keeping a tail reference makes it O(1).

questions.question: Why does LinkedList normally use more memory per element than ArrayList?
options: It always reserves capacity for extra nodes
It stores each element twice to allow fast reversal
It maintains a parallel index array
Every element needs a node object with prev and next
questions.explanation: ArrayList keeps bare references in one array, while LinkedList allocates a separate node object holding item, next and prev for each element.

questions.question: Why can iterating an ArrayList beat iterating a LinkedList even though both are O(n)?
options: ArrayList elements are contiguous, giving better cache locality
The JIT compiles ArrayList loops down to O(log n)
LinkedList recomputes size() on every step
LinkedList iterators copy the list before iterating
questions.explanation: Array elements sit in adjacent memory so cache lines and prefetching pay off, whereas linked nodes can be scattered across the heap.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a sentinel (dummy) head node in a linked list implementation?
options: It halves the memory used by the list
It makes get(i) run in constant time
It keeps the list sorted automatically
It removes special cases for insert and delete at the head
questions.explanation: With a sentinel every real node has a predecessor, so insertion and deletion need no null-head branch, which kills the classic edge-case bugs.

questions.question: head points to a chain of exactly 4 nodes. What value does count hold when this loop ends?
questions.explanation: The loop stops on the last node, so it counts links rather than nodes. Counting nodes needs the condition n != null.

questions.question: On a LinkedList of size n, what is the worst-case cost of add(index, e) at a middle index?
options: O(n), because the position must be walked to first
O(1), because links are simply rewired
O(log n), using an internal index cache
questions.explanation: Splicing the node itself is O(1), but LinkedList must first walk to the index from the nearer end, which is O(n) for a middle position.

questions.question: Why is ArrayDeque usually preferred over LinkedList for queue and stack use?
options: ArrayDeque permits null elements, LinkedList does not
ArrayDeque has lower per-element overhead and better locality
ArrayDeque is synchronized, so it is safer
ArrayDeque also supports get(i) in O(1)
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque stores elements in a circular array: no node object per element and far better cache behaviour. Neither class is synchronized.

z is appended at the end
questions.explanation: remove() clears the iterator's lastReturned element, so set() has nothing to replace and throws IllegalStateException until next() or previous() is called.

questions.question: This in-place reversal is broken. What is the defect?
options: prev should start at head instead of null
cur.next is overwritten before being saved, so the tail is lost
The condition should be cur.next != null
It reverses fine, only head is left pointing at the old first node
questions.explanation: cur.next is reassigned before the rest of the chain is stored, so cur jumps to the old prev and every node after head becomes unreachable.

questions.question: Inserting m elements at position k of a LinkedList: which approach costs O(k + m) instead of roughly O(m*k)?
options: Call add(k, e) in a loop
Call addFirst(e) m times, then rotate the list
Call listIterator(k) once and add through the iterator
Copy to an ArrayList, insert there, then copy back
questions.explanation: Each add(k, e) re-walks to position k, giving O(m*k). A single listIterator(k) walks once, after which every add at the cursor is O(1).
